operations.evidence: Outcome 14 applies where no named suspect has been identified; the crime is confirmed; the victim declines or is unable to support further police action to identify the offender
it must not be merged with outcome 16, where a suspect is identified; victim non-support is not proof that the offence did not occur
Outcome 15 applies where a named suspect has been identified; the victim supports police action; evidential difficulties prevent further action and can include a wanted suspect who cannot be traced
it must not be merged with victim-withdrawal outcomes; a wanted-but-untraced case is not a conviction or completed prosecution
Outcome 16 applies where a named suspect has been identified; the victim does not support or withdraws support from police action; the category is victim-based evidential difficulty
withdrawal must not be treated as evidence that the crime was false; it must remain separate from outcome 14 and outcome 15
Outcome 17 applies where a suspect has been identified; the prosecution time limit has expired; the category was introduced from April 2014
it applies only to offences with a prosecution time limit; expiry is a procedural outcome rather than a harm or safety measure
Outcome 18 applies where no suspect has been identified; the crime has been investigated as far as reasonably possible; the case is closed pending further investigative opportunities
closure does not mean the offence did not occur; future investigative opportunities can reopen activity
Outcome 19 is an NFIB-only fraud outcome; a fraud crime has been recorded; the NFIB assessment found insufficient lines of enquiry to allocate it for investigation
it must not be applied to non-NFIB offences; filing is not proof that the report was invalid
Outcome 20 applies where another body or agency will undertake further action; the victim or representative must be made aware of the action; the outcome was introduced from April 2015
the responsible external body is not automatically identified in aggregate statistics; the outcome is not equivalent to police inaction
Outcome 21 applies where a suspect is identified; further investigation could provide evidence sufficient for formal action; the police decide that further action is not in the public interest
it must not be merged with outcome 10 or CPS outcome 9 without definition checks; public-interest decisions are not severity rankings
Outcome 22 requires diversionary, educational or intervention activity; after that activity it is not in the public interest to take further action; collection was voluntary from April 2019
voluntary introduction affects early coverage; activity completion is not a conviction or universal success measure
outcomes 14 to 19 date from April 2014; outcome 20 dates from April 2015 and outcome 21 from January 2016; outcome 22 was voluntary from April 2019
time-series comparisons require outcome-specific start dates; availability must not be backfilled into earlier periods
the provisional YE March 2026 CSEW response rate is 48 percent; the rate is based on the issued sample; ONS states that it is lower than historical response rates
the response rate is provisional; response rate is not the same as estimate accuracy

ONS gives a pre-pandemic example response rate of 70 percent for YE March 2019; the March 2026 provisional response rate is substantially lower; the pandemic caused severe disruption to face-to-face fieldwork
the two years have different fieldwork contexts; the comparison does not by itself quantify non-response bias

CSEW weighting adjusts for possible non-response bias; the aim is to make the sample reflect the general population profile; ONS says further analysis is required to understand lower-response profile variation
weighting cannot guarantee removal of all non-response bias; residual uncertainty must remain visible

sample estimates differ from a full-population census result; sampling error is used to construct confidence intervals; confidence intervals express a range of plausible population values at a stated confidence level
point estimates must not be treated as exact counts; confidence intervals do not capture every non-sampling error
the face-to-face CSEW uses the Postal Address File as its sample frame; the frame covers household addresses in England and Wales; non-response is built into the sample process
the frame does not cover every non-household population; an address frame is not a parcel-risk inventory

the target sample for the 2025 to 2026 CSEW is 31,000 interviews per year; the target supports national and police-force-area estimation; the target is a design parameter rather than the achieved sample
target interviews must not be substituted for achieved interviews; sample size does not create parcel-level observations
the sample is designed to yield at least 585 interviews in each police force area; smaller police force areas are oversampled within the weighting design; PFA estimates remain survey estimates
585 is a design minimum rather than an exact achieved count for every release; PFA sample sizes do not support parcel-level inference
31,532 adult interviews were achieved for the 2024 to 2025 CSEW; the achieved count is reported separately from the 2025 to 2026 target; children's-survey participation is a separate component
the achieved count is edition-specific; adult interviews must not be combined with child interviews without separate bases
raw CSEW data are weighted for unequal selection probabilities; the adjustment includes household adult counts; it also accounts for oversampling and multi-household addresses
selection weights are not risk weights; weights must remain tied to the survey design
calibration weighting aligns the survey to known population totals; it adjusts for differential non-response; published CSEW percentages and rates use weighted data
calibration does not make the survey a census; unweighted and weighted values must not be mixed

ONS estimates that around 42 percent of CSEW-comparable crimes were reported by the public to police in YE March 2026; police recorded crime therefore omits many unreported offences; the estimate concerns comparable CSEW crimes
42 percent is not applicable to every offence type; the proportion is not a local reporting rate

the proportion reported to police varies considerably by offence type; recorded-crime fitness depends on reporting as well as recording; aggregate reporting proportions can conceal offence differences
a national average must not be assigned to each offence; reporting variation is not proof of force under-recording
police recorded crime can be used for local crime pattern analysis; it is useful for well-reported and well-recorded offences; homicide is a key example not covered by CSEW
local pattern use still requires geography and recording-quality controls; it does not support exact parcel attribution by itself
recorded crime is an important indicator of police workload; it shows where policing effort is being spent; workload interpretation is distinct from victimisation prevalence
high workload is not automatically high underlying crime; recording and enforcement activity affect workload measures

drug-possession recorded volumes are heavily influenced by police activity and priorities; for such offences recorded crime can indicate enforcement activity; the measure may not reflect underlying criminality directly
activity-sensitive categories must not be compared as pure prevalence; policy changes can create discontinuities
CSEW includes offences not reported to or recorded by police; it is widely viewed as an independent check on police figures; responsibility transferred from the Home Office to ONS in April 2012
CSEW has its own scope exclusions and sampling errors; independence does not make sources interchangeable
